title: Set a water meter with 10 pipe diameters of straight pipe before it and 5 after
instruction: Lay the water meter and the three pipe lengths end to end in the channel from the elbow to the valve, the first one against the elbow and every joint closed; the valve's union takes up the gap left at its end. Water flows from the elbow to the valve: point the meter's arrow toward the valve with its blue register on top, and leave at least 10 pipe diameters (250 mm) of straight pipe between the elbow and the meter and 5 (125 mm) between the meter and the valve. Let go and move clear.
context: Plumbers and pipefitters (O*NET 47-2152.00) and meter installers (49-9012.00) set velocity-type water meters (single-jet, Woltmann) where the flow reaching them is straight. ISO 4064-1 and OIML R 49 mark each meter with a flow-profile sensitivity class, for example U10 D5: at least 10 nominal diameters of straight pipe before the meter and 5 after it. Butted straights of the same bore count as straight pipe; only an elbow, valve or other flow disturber breaks a straight run. Makers' instructions set these lengths and plumbing codes require installing to them (IPC 303.2). Closer than that, the swirl and skewed profile from an elbow or valve shift the reading and the customer is billed wrongly for years; a meter fitted backwards reads backwards or not at all. A meter set is laid out from pre-cut straights so the meter falls in the right place, arrow downstream, register up. Bench model: 25 mm pipe, so 10 D = 250 mm and 5 D = 125 mm.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Water runs along -y, from the elbow on the left to the valve on the right. Fixed to the table: (1) Elbow: a copper-coloured metal block standing in for a 90-degree elbow, 40 x 40 x 40 mm, centred at x 30.0 cm, y +31.0 cm; its right-hand (-y) face, at y +29.0 cm, starts the run. A white plastic tile 20 x 20 x 1 mm lies centred on its top. (2) Supply pipe: a copper bar 60 mm (along x) x 25 x 25 mm, from x 32.0 to 38.0 cm, centred at y +31.0 cm, against the elbow's far face. (3) Valve: a brass block 40 x 40 x 40 mm centred at x 30.0 cm, y -31.0 cm; its left-hand (+y) face, at y -29.0 cm, ends the run, 580 mm from the elbow's face. A red painted-aluminium lever 10 mm (x) x 40 mm (y) x 6 mm lies centred on its top, along the pipe (open). (4) Two rails: grey aluminium strips 6 mm wide, 8 mm tall, 580 mm long along y (y -29.0 to +29.0 cm), their inner faces at x 28.15 and 31.85 cm: a channel 37 mm wide, 6 mm of play each side of a 25 mm part, its ends against the elbow and the valve. Loose, lying flat on the table along x: (5) Three pipe lengths: square aluminium tubes painted copper, 25 x 25 mm, 2 mm wall: 250 mm long, 0.12 kg, centred at x 36.0 cm, y -41.0 cm; 125 mm, 0.06 kg, centred at x 15.0 cm, y -42.0 cm; 75 mm, 0.035 kg, centred at x 15.0 cm, y +42.0 cm. (6) Water meter: one rigid body of 0.20 kg: a hollow brass body 100 x 25 x 25 mm (2 mm walls); on its top, centred, a blue painted-aluminium register block 40 mm (along the body) x 16 mm x 12 mm tall, leaving 30 mm of bare body at each end; on the register's top a white flow arrow of 3 mm thick plastic strips along the body, 30 mm long: a shaft 18 x 4 mm and a head of three 4 mm steps, 12, 8 and 4 mm wide. Its body is centred at x 26.0 cm, y +41.0 cm, along x, register up, arrow pointing +x (away from the arms). The parts total 550 mm, so a butted run leaves 30 mm at the valve. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Scored from the end state: each part's pose and, from the embodiment's state, each gripper's finger-tip point (between its tips) and tool point (13 mm back up it). A part is 'laid' when (a) it lies flat: for a pipe, the normal of its nearest long face is within 5 degrees of vertical (any of its four long faces may be down; either end may lead); for the meter, its register is on top and its up axis within 5 degrees of vertical; (b) its long axis is within 5 degrees of y seen from above; (c) its centre is within 8 mm of x 30.0 cm (between the rails, not on one); (d) its lowest point is within 3 mm of the table top (not on a rail or on another part). A part's ends are its two end-face centres; the parts are taken in order of their centres from the elbow. The elbow joint runs from the elbow's face (y +29.0 cm) to the first part's near end; each part-to-part joint from one part's far end to the next part's near end (negative if they overlap). The gap at the valve, after the last part, is not checked (the union takes up 0 to 30 mm). The run is 'closed' when all four parts are laid and every checked joint is between -2 mm and +5 mm (-2 mm allows for contact penetration in the simulation). U, the straight run before the meter, is from the elbow's face to the meter's inlet (upstream) end face; D, after it, from the meter's outlet end face to the valve's face. Laid, the meter's arrow points along the run within 5 degrees: toward the valve (downstream) or toward the elbow (backwards). 'Let go' means each gripper can be read and its finger line, from its finger-tip point 38 mm back up the gripper, is at least 65 mm from every part's outline box (the meter's is 40 mm tall, register and arrow included), so no open finger (60.4 mm out from that line) touches a part at any tilt. A gripper that cannot be read on a step has not let go. Score: 0 if a gripper has not let go; else 0 if the run is not closed (fewer than four parts laid, a joint over 5 mm or under -2 mm, a part on a rail or on another part, off the line or across it, the meter on its side or upside down); else 0.25 if the meter is backwards; else 1.0 if U is at least 245 mm and D at least 120 mm; else 0.5 (one straight run short; both cannot be). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0; every end state maps to exactly one. The score is read at the last step: the trial ends early once the 1.0 conditions have held for 1 s with no part's end-face centre having travelled more than 2 mm in all over the last 0.5 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. From the elbow, the orders that score 1.0 are 75-250-meter-125, 250-75-meter-125, 250-meter-75-125 and 250-meter-125-75 (U 250 or 325 mm and D 230 or 155 mm with joints at 0); 250-125-meter-75 leaves D at most 111 mm (0.5), and any order with the 250 after the meter leaves U at most 215 mm (0.5). In a real trial: a tape from the elbow's face to the meter's inlet face and from its outlet face to the valve's; a 5 mm feeler gauge must not enter any joint, the elbow's included; a photo from above for the arrow, the register, the parts in the channel and both grippers 65 mm clear.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with the simulator's default friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). Square tubes stand in for round 25 mm pipe so they lie still and butt face to face; joints are butted, not soldered or threaded, and a joint of 5 mm or less counts as made up. The valve's union is not modelled: the 0-30 mm gap at the valve stands for its take-up. No water flows: the straight runs are checked as a fitter checks them, with a tape. The meter is one rigid body with a raised register and arrow.
reset_notes: Put the three pipes and the meter back flat on the table along x: the 250 mm pipe centred at x 36.0 cm, y -41.0 cm; the 125 mm pipe at x 15.0 cm, y -42.0 cm; the 75 mm pipe at x 15.0 cm, y +42.0 cm; the meter's body centred at x 26.0 cm, y +41.0 cm, register up, arrow pointing away from the arms. The elbow, supply pipe, valve and rails are fixed. Nothing is consumed.
